utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We welcome you all back, and we are glad to see that people have managed to be here. There was some uncertainty, obviously, about that. We are able to carry on as planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Djurdjic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. Simovic. Our next witness is Mr. Zoran Simovic. Mr. Simovic, as we speak the same language, please try to speak slowly so that we can get a good transcript and a good translation. Therefore, please answer slowly and make a pause between my question and your answer. For the transcript, could you please tell us your full name and your personal details.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Simovic. I was born on the 10th of February, 1961 in Novi Pazar. I completed the secondary school for police academy in Sremska Kamenica. I started to work in 1979, and I also completed the college for the interior and then the faculty --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what school at university level he completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, could you please repeat for the transcript the schools that you completed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the secondary school for the interior, the police academy in Sremska Kamenica in 1979. Then I completed the college, the police college in Belgrade, and at the university of Belgrade I graduated from the school of defectology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what your present job is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I currently -- am currently the assistant commander at the gendarmerie command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is that part or within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The gendarmerie is the unit of the police of the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, briefly something about your career.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: When I graduated from the secondary police academy in 1979 I began work as a policeman at the city secretariat of the interior in Belgrade. At the Belgrade SUP, I worked as a police officer and instructor for special physical, up until 1986. On April 1st in 1986, I was transferred to the R SUP of Serbia, the Republic SUP of Serbia to the special operations unit which at the time was attached to the detachment for security at the R SUP, the republican SUP. In 1992, I was appointed commander of the special SAJ unit in Belgrade where I remained until 1999. After 1999 I was transferred to the police administration, and I remained there until 2001 when the gendarmerie was established and then I was transferred to the gendarmerie where I remain to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3, lines 3 and 4, it says Special Operations Unit and, in fact, it should be Special Activities Unit. In 1998 and 1999, what positions were you on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I've mentioned that between 1992 and 1999 I was the commander of a special anti-terrorist unit of the Serbia MUP for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us a few words about the organisation and functioning of the Serbia MUP SAJ unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The SAJ unit of the Republic of Serbia MUP was established in 1978 as a special actions unit of the ministry of the Republic of Serbia until 1992 when it was dubbed SAJ. In the meantime, it had changed its name on several occasions. In 1976, [as interpreted] the minister of the interior, Mr. Sokolovic established a especially anti-terrorist units of the Republic of Serbia MUP, which as part of its composition had three units, the Belgrade SAJ unit, the Pristina SAJ unit, and the Novi Sad SAJ unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. In transcript it says in 1976 minister Sokolovic established this special unit. Could you just tell us what year actually it was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, actually it was in 1986, or rather 1996, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please show the witness D401. And, Your Honours, could we please provide the witness the binder with the documents so that we could actually move along more speedily?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, I will mention the tab in your document binder, and before us, we will see in a moment document D401.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a technical problem at the moment. If you could wait, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are going to dwell on this document for awhile, so we can actually have it on the monitors later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, tell us, please, in keeping with this decision by Minister Sokolovic, could you describe the structure and organisation of the SAJ unit. The decision is dated April 5, 1996.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, Minister Sokolovic issued this written decision to establish a special anti-terrorist unit. Under number 1 it says that the special anti-terrorist unit is established as a separate unit within the sector of the interior of the RJB. It will have its seats in Belgrade, Pristina, and Novi Sad. In other words, the SAJ command was in the building of the Republic of Serbia Ministry of the Interior at Mesa Milosa 103. The command was there -- the command of all three units was there. The Ministry of the Interior of Serbia has three SAJ units: Belgrade, Novi Sad, and Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, in 1998 and 1999 who was the commander of the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: From the time when the SAJ was established in 1992 up until 1999, the commander of the SAJ was Colonel Zivko Trajkovic. And I've already said he was the commander of the Belgrade SAJ in Belgrade, he was the commander of the Belgrade SAJ in Belgrade -- he was the commander of the SAJ in Belgrade, Stalevic was the commander in Pristina, and Curcic was the commander in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we seem to be having some inconsistency about the date. Page 4, line 20 speaks of the decision of the minister of the 5th of April, 1996. Page 5, line 7 speaks of 1992. Is one of those wrong, or is there some explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain it, Your Honours. This decision of April 5, 1996, actually put out of force a decision on the SAJ of 1992. Such a unit called a SAJ was first established in 1992 under that name, and then in 1996, Minister Sokolovic established a different structure and tasks of this unit that was called a special anti-terrorist unit, short for SAJ, S-A-J. Your Honours, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, who was the commander of the Belgrade SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Belgrade SAJ, actually, that was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. What were the tasks of the SAJ unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The SAJ was entrusted the most complex tasks by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. Its tasks were to protect the republic, its citizens, and especially in situations of hijacking of airplanes or other means of transportation, hostage situations, arrests of dangerous individuals and criminals where there is an expectation that fire-arms might be used, as well as in situations where there are major disturbances of law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you -- were you also trained for preventing and fighting terrorism?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the primary task of this unit was to fight terrorism, and this in the aftermath of the events in 1996 [as interpreted] in Germany when the Israeli sportsmen were killed, and then there was also a hijacking of the then YAT plane so that the then-Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia decided to establish a unit to fight terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the transcript it reads that this crime against the athletes at the Olympic games in Germany was in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Mr. Simovic, who decided to use this unit to handle these tasks as you mentioned them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The decision to employ the unit could be made only by the minister of the interior, and he did this via the chief of sector because the SAJ unit was part of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the operational commander of the units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The operational commander of the unit was the unit commander. In fact, the SAJ commander who received orders would then decide which unit to entrust with a certain task, whether that would be the SAJ Belgrade, Novi Sad, or Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On line 21 on this page it says that the decision to use this unit is made by the ministry?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, actually, it's the minister who takes that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, what was the structure and how was the Belgrade SAJ organised, the unit at whose head you were?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The structure of the unit whose commander I was was as follows: It had its command, three platoons, each platoon had three squads which numbered approximately 100 men, and the operational composition of the unit was between 50 and 60 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it approximately the same structure in the SAJ Pristina and the SAJ Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: All three units had an identical structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the complement, the fullness of the complement of the SAJ, especially during the anti-terrorist operation and the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer operations of 1998 and the war in 1999, in 1998 the SAJ had an almost full complement while in 1999 pursuant to a decision made by the minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, the SAJ Novi Sad was abolished in 1998 so that removed one-third of the personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You told us that the base, the headquarters of the SAJ was in Belgrade, was in the Mesa Milosa Street, but where was the seat of your unit, your base?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: My unit was based in Batajnica near Belgrade at the 13 May centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, during the 1999 war, where was your unit employed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: During the war in 1999 on the 23rd of March, 1999, the unit was sent to the province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us who planned the activities of your unit during the war when you were in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: All the operations on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, that means from July until early October, and during the war, were planned by the headquarters for anti-terrorism which had its base at the SUP -- at the MUP Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said July until early October, which year do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I mean 1998 because the headquarters for combat against terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija was established in June that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how do you know that these headquarters were formed in June, this staff was formed in June?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in regular situations, Mr. Trajkovic and I had two meetings a month, and depending on the situation, it could be more. However, at one of these meetings, Mr. Trajkovic informed all the commanders, that is, me, Stalevic and Curcic, that a decision had been made by the minister to establish the staff for combat against terrorism for Kosovo and Metohija that he himself was a member of that staff, that the General Sreten Lukic was appointed head of the staff, David Gajic from the public security sector was appointed his deputy, and another member of the staff was Milorad Ulemek, also known as Legija, commander of the JSO unit, unit for special operations that belonged to the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who gave you your assignments during these anti-terrorist activities from July to early October 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier, all the assignments were issued by the staff, and I personally received my assignments from my commander, Mr. Trajkovic. When I say staff, I mean the staff for combat against terrorism for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you proceed with the next question, I'm wondering, Your Honour, if perhaps we could clarify what the record at page 8, lines 23 and 24, if I probably heard correctly or not. It says, David Gajic from the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the Prosecutor. Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I said the head of the staff was General Lukic, and his deputy was David Gajic from the state security sector and so was Milorad Lukovic [as interpreted] also known as Legija, he was also from the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To clarify the transcript in the same line, what was Mr. Zivko Trajkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who established the staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If e-court is now working, I would like to call up D106?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And for you, it's tab 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It doesn't appear yet to be working.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's still not that great a problem. I think we can explain in another way. The witness has the relevant decision before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is the decision of the minister dated 19 July 1998 awarding certain rewards or decorations for members of the PJP, SAJ, and JSO. Were you familiar with this decision when it was made?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because we were commanders of our respective units, and we made lists and gave them to Commander Trajkovic, and he carried them to the staff so that these remunerations could be distributed to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To which sector did the PJP and SAJ units belong?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The PJP and SAJ belonged to the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about the JSO, the unit for special operations, which was a police unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a special unit of the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can't have it in e-court, but I'd like to review D107. It's binder [as interpreted] number 3 for you, witness. It's a dispatch from the ministry staff from Pristina dated 20th October, 1998. Could you tell us to whom was it sent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I see it was signed by the head of the staff, Major-General Sreten Lukic, but it was sent to the units of the PJP, the SAJ, and the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what does the heading say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Commanders of the PJP, SAJ, and JSO, and chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Chiefs where?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The chiefs of secretariats in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We see that this is an order to pay out those rewards and remunerations from the 17th of September until 11 October. Was it usual to receive such dispatches during anti-terrorist operations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were they acted upon?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And did people actually receive these remunerations, these bonuses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything written in the dispatches had to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said the activities were planned by the MUP staff in Pristina, but would you tell us how you as commander of the SAJ Belgrade and other commanders of the SAJ received your assignments during the 1999 war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: All the plans for the employment of our units and the assignments in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija for the police were issued by the staff for combat against terrorism. Our commander, Trajkovic, was a member of that staff and he was also our commander. He, as a commander, received assignments from the staff that would be an extract on a topographic map with the axis of operation drawn in. With that map, he would convene a meeting of all the three commanders in the period while Novi Sad was still within our complement. That Commander Stalevic and I would work in detail on the plan and then he would give us specific assignments individually according to the axis that had to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just tell us, when exactly was that ministerial decision whereby the SAJ Novi Sad ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was the decision of Minister Trajkovic, [as interpreted] and I believe it was towards the end of December that the SAJ Novi Sad was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So during the war, which units made up the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, the SAJ or the SAJ command were made up of SAJ Pristina and SAJ Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you explain technically how it worked receiving assignments from the staff during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Assignments were received by Commander Trajkovic who either went to the staff or would send the courier to get the assignments or a courier came from the staff to Commander Trajkovic bringing assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Line 2, page 12, who was the minister of the interior towards the end of 1998, the one who abolished that unit of the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 the minister was Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: During the war in 1999, to whom would you report after an operation was completed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: During the war in 1999 both I and Commander Stalevic did not submit written reports, but would upon each operation completed analyse the operation together with Commander Trajkovic, and he would then report to the staff. Whether he did it in writing or orally, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: While we are on the subject, could you tell us during those anti-terrorist operations in the summer of 1998, how did reporting after operations completed work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and during the war we acted exactly as I just described. I'm sorry, Your Honours, if I can just add. When I say 1998, that means the period from the establishment of the staff for combat against terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. I'm looking at another thing though. I see on the transcript the word "operation" used constantly whereas I use the word "action".

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, you told us that towards the end of December 1998, the SAJ Novi Sad was abolished. How did that affect your operational capacity, I mean the capacity of the SAJ as a unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I said before, the operational capacity of the SAJ was reduced by about 30 per cent because one unit was gone and that meant around 100 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That was towards the end of 1998. Could you tell us if any steps were made to improve the operational capacity of the SAJ in view of the fact that this unit in Novi Sad was abolished and in view also of the security situation that prevailed in the beginning of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Since the SAJ was involved in assignments in Kosovo and the operations in 1998 involved a large number of losses, deaths, and injuries, and once the SAJ Novi Sad was abolished, our operational capacity was reduced, diminished. At some of the meetings with Mr. Trajkovic we discussed options for replenishing, reinforcing our units. When I say "our units", I mean SAJ, not SAJ Belgrade. Since the regular procedure for admission into a special anti-terrorist unit is long, the SAJ recruits from the regular police force, preferably the best police officers. And then the procedure of admission takes several months. And since we didn't have that time in this particular case, Mr. Trajkovic told us in our discussions that we need to find a possibility to recruit from the reserve police force from the reserve of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please, what was the security situation in February and March 1998 -- 1999, in other words, before the 20th of March; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that it was very complex. We were expecting a NATO strike against Serbia, and Mr. Trajkovic at one of the meetings, I believe this was in the second half of February, said that the minister had called for a greater involvement of the SAJ in the following period, and on that occasion, he discussed this with a certain Mrgud, whom he knew, in terms of there existing an amount or a number of men in -- from Srem who had moved from Croatia to Serbia, and that if they met all the requirements to be admitted into the reserve force, that then this should be discussed with the minister via the chief of sector so that they can immediately proceed with the procedure to recruit these new men into the reserve force -- police force. What I mentioned here, that the chief of sector had to discuss this with the minister, that was a reference to the fact that Mr. Trajkovic could not do this directly. He could not discuss this with the minister directly. It could only be done through the chief of sector. And the minister was the only one who could actually take this decision on recruitment of personnel into the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Trajkovic tell you anything about these men that he felt should be admitted into the reserve force of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Trajkovic? Trajkovic told us that he knew a certain number of these men, that he had met them in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem while he was a member of the Territorial Defence of that territory, of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, was the SAJ unit actually reinforced by this reserve force, the reserve MUP unit? And if so, how did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just point one thing out. The special anti-terrorist unit, the SAJ, did not have its own reserve force, and it never had had it. That is why we explored this possibility of having a regular reserve force attached, the regular reserve force from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia attached to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I was actually asking you whether that reserve force was actually attached to the SAJ unit, and if so, how did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I understood your question the first time around, but I was waiting for the interpreters to do their job. On the 26th, I believe it was on the 26th of March, on the axis of operation where we were employed, Commander Trajkovic said to me and Mr. Stalevic, that the reserve force of the Republic of Serbia MUP, which was supposed to be attached to our unit, was in Prolom Banja. In the evening, on the 26th of March, 1999, Trajkovic went that night in the direction of Podujevo. I don't know where he went. On the following day, on the 27th in the morning hours, I believe it was around 11.00 but I cannot recall the time with precision, Mr. Trajkovic called us on the radio from Podujevo and informed us that in Bradas village he would come to meet us, and he meant Stalevic and myself, and this was where our operation was supposed to end. He called Mr. Stalevic and asked him to go to the main road to meet him there in order to escort him to the centre of Bradas village where I was waiting for them. Not far from where I was in the centre of Bradas village, some 30 metres or so away, Mr. Stalevic's jeep drove by, and behind his jeep was Commander Trajkovic's jeep, which actually ran on to -- into an anti-tank mine. There was a very loud explosion, a blast. I saw thick black smoke, and this jeep was blown up in this blast and thrown off the road. I ran towards the place where the anti-tank mine was set off and Commander Stalevic, who was in the immediate vicinity, had already got off his vehicle, and as Mr. Markovic, the doctor of our unit, was in the vehicle with him, they were already there on site, and they were administering first aid to the wounded. However, unfortunately, Aleksic, Mr. Radovan Aleksic, died on the spot. There was no help for him. And Mr. Trajkovic and his driver, Basara, Zoran and the analyst Petrovic, Nikola were taken by Dr. Dragan after first aid was administered to the hospital in Pristina where they were to undergo a detailed examination, and the body of the late Aleksic was transferred to pathology, to the forensic pathology department at the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us the doctor's name, please, for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Dragan Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, could you tell us, please, what you did next?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: After Dr. Dragan took the wounded men and drove off toward Pristina, Commander Stalevic and I went to Podujevo, to the OUP. Stalevic telephoned the staff from the Podujevo OUP and informed them of the incident. In the meantime, Dr. Markovic conveyed to us by radio that Commander Trajkovic was slightly wounded, that he went to the anti-terrorist staff in Pristina, and -- headquarters in Pristina and that he would then come to the Podujevo OUP to meet with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you something. What happened with your units, your own and Mr. Stalevic's unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Our units were deployed at Podujevo, and they were resting pending the next assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the wounding on the 27th of March, 1999, did you see Commander Trajkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic was not wounded. He was injured. I saw him around 1700 hours in Podujevo. He came to see Sava and me. He had the stiff collar around his neck. He didn't have any fractures. He just had a contusion, a concussion of the head, and he said to Stalevic that both units should remain in Podujevo. And as he was unable to go and take over the reserve force unit which was in Prolom Banja because had he to go to Belgrade to organise the burial of the late Aleksic, he assigned me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said here "Sava." Could you tell us the last name of this person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, out of habit, I will probably use the name Sava because that is the habitual usage, but that is the commander of the Pristina SAJ, Radislav Stalevic, whom everybody calls Sava and whom we all know by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, you told us that Commander Trajkovic told you that he was going to Belgrade to organise the burial of your dead member, and you were assigned to go to Prolom Banja to actually take over the reserve force. Did you do as you were instructed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I complied with Mr. Trajkovic’s order because he told me that after he was given assistance, medical assistance, he had been to the MUP staff for combat against terrorism in Pristina and that they agreed, or rather they gave permission to go to the reserve force unit at Prolom Banja. And I went together with Mr. Trajkovic, well, actually, we each went in our own vehicles because when you go from Podujevo in the direction of Belgrade, you go actually on the same road, some 15 kilometres, and then I split and I went right towards Prolom Banja where this reserve force of the Republic of Serbia MUP was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what happened in Prolom Banja when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Prolom Banja, I was instructed by Mr. Trajkovic to look for a certain Boca. His name is Slobodan Medic, and that he was with this reserve force of the MUP but that in an oral agreement between him and Mr. Trajkovic, he was in a way responsible for this force. I met Mr. Medic and was introduced to him because that was the first time that I saw him. I hadn't met them before. He asked me about Djila referring to Commander Zivko Trajkovic. I told him what had happened and that Mr. Trajkovic had to go to Belgrade and that I came to arrange for the next day, the 28th, for them to be ready and that I would come to pick them up in order to escort them to Kosovo and Metohija to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On line 24 on page 18, it says he asked me about Djila?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, not Djila, Zile. Z.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Z-i-l-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very well, there is no other way that we can spell this. We can just spell it with a Z but, in fact, it's Zile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did members of the reserve force while they were in Prolom Banja have a vehicle that they had arrived in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were transported by buses from Belgrade to Prolom Banja, and the same buses were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Simovic, tell us, please, did you have transport vehicles in your units that could be used by these reserve -- members of the reserve force of the MUP once they were attached to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the Novi Sad SAJ was disbanded, all of its equipment was then transferred to the Belgrade and Pristina SAJs so that we had armoured trucks, TAM 110 and 150 trucks that were for transport of personnel in certain situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were these trucks on the 27th and the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Some of them were with us, with the unit, and others were at the forward command post of SAJ Pristina in Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: These armoured trucks, is that what you meant, were they armoured, bulletproof?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not factory made like that, but they were later provided with an armour that stops rifle ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: These trucks that we were discussing, were they at your disposal throughout the 1999 war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was equipment that belonged to the SAJ command. Now, how it would be distributed between Belgrade and Pristina did not matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What happened after their discussion with Mr. Medic in Prolom Banja? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I told Mr. Medic that between 4.00 and 5.00 a.m. I would come to pick them up. And I went to Podujevo where my unit was deployed to talk some more with Mr. Stalevic because I was supposed to go to Belgrade after bringing that reserve to the funeral of Mr. Aleksic, and I had some outstanding operational matters to discuss with Mr. Stalevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was going on on the 28th of March 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th, as I said, I went with my driver and body-guard to Prolom Banja. They were waiting in their buses. I went ahead of their two buses to Podujevo and upon arrival, I told Mr. Medic and members of the reserve unit not to leave the buses until accommodation is provided for them, and then Medic and I went to the Podujevo OUP where Commander Stalevic was waiting for us to discuss the following steps. We got into Podujevo, and after awhile I heard two long volleys of fire from automatic weapons. I ran outside because I had had a feeling that something bad had happened. And indeed, some 300 metres from OUP Podujevo, I saw a group of my own unit members and ran towards them. When I got there, I found Dr. Dragan Markovic giving first aid to wounded civilians. There were a few more members of the SAJ who were helping the doctor in this job, and I did my best to organise ambulances urgently to transport the wounded people to the hospital in Pristina. One of my subordinate commanding officers, platoon Commander Vulevic, informed me that members of the reserve unit, whom I had brought and who had been supposed to stay on the buses, had fired on civilians. I did not see who fired, nor were my own unit members able to tell me. Once I had organised those ambulances for the wounded, I was told that there were fatalities, and I decided to take back that reserve unit to Prolom Banja. I issued an order to my own unit members that they take back to the bus everyone they find, and when I got to Podujevo, where Mr. Stalevic was present too, I told Mr. Medic to go back to the bus with members of the reserve force and return to Prolom Banja. While my people were collecting, gathering the members of their return unit and returning them to their buses, I was in OUP Podujevo and discussed with some of the officers there how to take all the necessary steps to secure the scene of the crime and do an on-site investigation. The OUP Podujevo informed an investigating judge. I informed the MUP staff for combat against terrorism located in Pristina about the decisions I had taken, namely to return that unit back to Prolom Banja, and I also informed the head of sector, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, in Belgrade, because I could not reach my own Commander Trajkovic on his cell phone. And since I was returning that unit to the territory of Serbia, and the whole of the MUP in Belgrade was relocated in view of the air-strikes, I did not know where each of the administrations were temporarily located, I needed to inform someone to take care of this reserve unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said an investigating judge was informed and there was an on-site investigation headed by an investigating judge, and you said that the competent police authorities filed their criminal reports and that the criminal proceedings were instituted against the persons who had then at that time been found to have perpetrated this -- crime in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... or to the Court where it is that the witness said all of that which you just recited?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said an investigating judge was informed, and I asked, was an investigating judge informed, and did the competent authorities in the police start proceedings against persons whom they had found to have perpetrated this crime in Podujevo. I don't see the problem. The witness told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it your proposition, Mr. Stamp, that this goes beyond what the witness actually said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it goes way beyond what the witness said. I suspect the witness will say it, but counsel shouldn't give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you have anticipated a great deal of what the witness might say if asked, Mr. Djurdjic. If you want this evidence from the witness, you need to explore it from him in the ordinary way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said an investigating judge had been informed by OUP Podujevo. Do you know if an on-site investigation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Already you are anticipating more than the witness has actually said. I suspect it's in your head as what ought to have been said, but it hasn't been said. If you want to have details of an investigating judge being informed and acting, you need to get it from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know after you informed OUP Podujevo of the incident which measures were then taken?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I informed OUP Podujevo so that they can take the following steps, further steps, but I don't know what further steps were taken because by that time I was no longer in Podujevo. I had immediately left for Belgrade. I escorted the reserve unit to the fork leading to Prolom Banja, and I continued on to Belgrade to attend the funeral of the late Aleksic. I informed the OUP of what had happened, that they needed to organise further investigative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what OUP Podujevo did about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I didn't because I was no longer in Podujevo. I had already left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But did you find out later?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: After I returned from that funeral, I learned that an on-site investigation had been carried out, that the investigating judge had come to the scene of the crime, that officers of the OUP Podujevo had been to Prolom Banja and taken certain steps. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone was prosecuted in relation to this incident in Podujevo on the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know it was reported in the media, and I had been invited to provide a statement in the case. There was a prosecution, and the perpetrators were arrested, not all of them at the same time, but depending on how evidence was collected but all the -- those involved in this incident had been prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Belgrade after you left on that 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Not long, a day or perhaps two. I went there just for the funeral, and I can't remember whether the body of the late Aleksic was transferred from Pristina on the 29th or the 30th. But as soon as this funeral was over, I went back to Kosovo and Metohija because my unit was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And do you know when commander Trajkovic arrived in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think Mr. Trajkovic arrived some seven days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Seven days after what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: After he left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honours, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic, it is. Could I say that searching back over the record by Judge Fluegge, some of what you thought you had asked, you had asked. You were partly right, and we were partly right. Sorry about that. We now adjourn for the first break. We resume at 11.00. A Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, before the break we discussed your return to Kosovo and Metohija from Belgrade during the war in 1999. Tell us, please, did you continue with your assignments together with your unit in KiM after you returned, after the funeral of your colleague in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Belgrade I stopped by the forward command post of the SAJ unit, which was in Gracanica, because the NATO air-strikes had begun and the SAJ command had been transferred, so that I went to the forward command post in order to determine or establish where exactly my unit was. At that point in time, my unit was deployed at Kosovo Polje where the forward base of the SAJ was located. Commander Stalevic too was in Kosovo Polje, and then we just resumed our assign -- our tasks, carrying out our tasks as assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the course of your further activities during the war and after your return, what was the -- what were the operational capabilities of the SAJ unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the SAJ was an exhausted unit. We did not have a sufficient number of men because one of our units had been disbanded, and we absolutely needed to improve our manpower levels and replenish our ranks. When I arrived soon after me Commander Trajkovic arrived too, and at one of the meetings that we had, Commander Stalevic and I raised this issue to see whether there was a possibility for actually getting more men for our unit. Mr. Trajkovic, as he was a member of the staff, was in regular communication with the staff, and he mentioned this problem as well. In the meantime, he suggested that Sava and I, or actually for our needs that the reserve force of the MUP be re-activated, which on the 28th in Podujevo had done what it had done. He said that he was now present, that he, too, would meet them, and that they would actually purge the ranks from those men who took -- who participated in the unfortunate incident in Podujevo and that he was responsible for them. A few days later, we asked him whether there was any news in that respect, and he told us that the staff was in agreement, and that through the chief of sector, the minister had approved their deployment, and the police administration was assigned the task to equip them and that we could expect their arrival in Kosovo and Metohija in a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they eventually arrive, those members of the reserve force of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the reserve force, I can't remember the exact date, but it would have been toward the end of April, arrived at our forward command in Kosovo Polje, the forward command of the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what tasks were members of the reserve force of the MUP assigned when they were attached to your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the MUP reserve force were not assigned the tasks that regular members of the SAJ were assigned. We employed them for guard duty, for holding the lines that we had reached in the course of our operations, and in some instances where it was necessary, they were also assigned some easier tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did members of the MUP reserve force participate in activities conducted by your operational teams?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Members of the reserve force could never work together with the operative or technical teams of the SAJ members. They could only carry out tasks that were assigned within their own reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did a certain number of men from the reserve force, were they attached to your SAJ unit in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of them were assigned to the SAJ in Belgrade and some to the SAJ in Pristina. Once the members of the reserve force were attached to my unit, and this was in Kosovo Polje, I organised a meeting with these men. I hadn’t – I didn’t recognise any of them as being a participant in the unfortunate event in Podujevo. What I wanted to know was that they had all done their military service because that was a requirement for all members of the MUP reserve force. They would have had to have done their military service. And based on what military branch they had served in and what occupational specialty they had while doing their military service, they would be used in order to establish groups or teams that were -- that would then be capable of carrying out certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did members of the reserve force take part in any of your activities during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an action, a major operation in the area of Jezerska Planina where they took part together with my unit in an action, and they carried out all the tasks they were assigned properly in a disciplined manner and efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than that one action, were members of the reserve force also employed in some other activities of yours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: After this action was completed, and it was completed on the 9th of May, members of the Republic of Serbia MUP reserve force were sent back to Belgrade and disbanded because there was no longer any need for their employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From that time on when they returned to Belgrade up until the end of the war, were they ever resubordinated to the SAJ unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Once they returned on the 9th of May, they left Kosovo, and they were no longer on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In other words, they were sent back to their homes. Now, this reserve force, I don't know exactly the date, but they were disbanded by pursuant to a decision of the minister and the reserve force that had been attached to our unit was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From that time when they returned to Belgrade up until the end of the war, were they ever again attached or resubordinated to the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of 1999, were you aware that any member of the reserve force that was attached to the SAJ had committed or was committing or committed any criminal offences in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know of any such criminal offences, but in order for someone to become a member of the reserve force of the MUP, such a member would have had to apply for the reserve force and would have to be processed according to the same procedure as any member of the regular reserve force. So that they would not be eligible if they committed any criminal offence or had any criminal record. So that when the members of the reserve force came to Kosovo and Metohija, I never suspected any of them of having committed any criminal offence because all of those checks would have had to be done in Belgrade in the course of the application procedure. The MUP in Belgrade would check the criminal records, they would check the court records.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, what was your relationship with General Vlastimir Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: We had a professional relationship. In other words, we had official ties and contacts but nothing out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings where he was present?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I attended meetings where the chief of sector was also present, but this was before the events in 1998 and 1999 when, as a commander of the special unit, when I needed to obtain certain equipment, I had occasion to have contacts with the chief of sector and sometimes, for instance, we would send our men for training abroad and so forth. So we only had official contact, nothing other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998 during anti-terrorist activities conducted in the summer of 1998, did you have occasion to meet General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 during the summer operations, I saw him on several occasions in Kosovo and Metohija. I can't remember exactly how many, three or four times perhaps, and even on one occasion on an axis of operation where we were engaged in Malisevo he came to visit us. The driver was driving his vehicle, he was with Commander Trajkovic, with Savo, and me. He asked us how the operation was developing. He asked whether we had any casualties. He asked us about the men. So just normal questions. He stayed with us some two to three hours, I don't know exactly how many. But as for any other occasions, I really can't recall because a lot time has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to executing these anti-terrorist operations in the summer, have you ever received any assignments from Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: We did not receive any assignments from Mr. Djordjevic, nor did Mr. Trajkovic while he was with us. We received our assignments exclusively from the staff for combat against terrorism for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war in 1999 when you were in Kosovo and Metohija, did you have occasion to meet with Mr. Djordjevic, General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija I did not meet with Mr. Djordjevic. I met with him on the 12th of May, 1999, in Belgrade in the newly relocated MUP because it was at the time when I was promoted into colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where was the SAJ base in Belgrade, the Belgrade unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The Belgrade unit? I said at the beginning that the base of the SAJ Belgrade was at the so-called 13 May centre in Batajnica, which is a suburb of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you learned that in that base of the SAJ in Batajnica there were bodies buried?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: About the bodies buried on the territory of the SAJ base, I found out after my return from Kosovo after the agreement had been signed when my unit left Kosovo, and my unit and the SAJ Pristina and the command of the SAJ all had their bases destroyed by the bombing, so we were all relocated to the 13 May centre. My subordinate commander, commander of the 3rd Platoon, Zoran Djokovic told me about it. He said, Boss, I have to tell you, and I already told Commander Trajkovic, just behind the perimeter of the target training-ground there are bodies buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Since Mr. Trajkovic and the whole command of the SAJ was there -- in fact, first of all, I couldn't believe what Djokovic was saying. I went to see Trajkovic and said, Is this true what Djokovic told me? Trajkovic said, Yes, it's true. The minister has been informed and don't you worry, it's none of your concern. I left completely dazed in disbelief that something like that could have happened in my centre, and I say "my centre" because we had taken over that centre from the federal Secretariat of the Interior, and still I couldn't muster the courage to go and see where those bodies were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: During the war, were you based in the 13 May centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not our base. During the period when there was a state of war, Djokovic and the other members of the SAJ who guarded the base had relocated the headquarters and the base so that apart from the guards, there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is when you conduct training, when you conducted training, did you conduct any training behind that para-pit of the target training-ground?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think I said earlier that this part of the compound was never used for any sort of training. It's completely covered by underbrush, although, it is a part of the territory of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, in our case we have already heard Mr. Zivko Trajkovic who was commander of the SAJ in 1998 and 1999. He has already testified, and I would like to put to you some passages from his testimony and ask you to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we get page 9087 of our transcript. 28 September 2009. The number is 90, 9087.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, witness Trajkovic said in lines 1 through 6: "In the period from the 24th," -- you will get the transcript in English so you don't need to look at it. I will be reading to you in Serbian. "From the 24th when the NATO intervention began in Kosovo, I contacted Mr. Djordjevic, and he told me that one combat unit was ready to join us. At that time, as we were involved in carrying out another specific task, I could not give any kind of approval, and I said that we should wait until completion of this action that was underway and only then would we be able to accept this unit in a proper manner because we needed vehicles for them, and we had no vehicles resubordinated to us for that purpose, and we couldn't drive them around Kosovo in buses." And then on page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 9089 and 9090. I'm repeating the pages 9089, line 25, and page 9090, lines 1 through 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The answer of Mr. Trajkovic: "Well, first of all, as our units were quite mobile, we frequently moved from one area to another. So in order to be able to accept them, we had to review together with the staff the possibility to have some field vehicles bring these people to the place where they would be quartered. That's what I had in mind first." Now, I'd like to ask you, Mr. Simovic, on the 28th and 29th of March, did you have any transportation vehicles in the field available to drive around these reservists if they should be resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, they arrived on the 28th on buses. In Podujevo our unit had trucks to transport its own personnel, and we got these trucks, as I said before, when the SAJ Novi Sad had been disbanded. We received part of their equipment. And another part of the equipment was the forward post in Gracanica. So we had vehicles. As far as weapons are concerned, they had been issued weapons by the police administration, and they had already arrived in Kosovo with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pages I quoted were different. They were 9089, line 25, and page 9090, lines 1 through 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, I will now put to you another passage from the evidence of Mr. Trajkovic on page 9092, lines 5 through 7, and lines 8 through 14. The Prosecutor's question was: "What happened with these men that Mr. Djordjevic discussed with you or that you discussed with Mr. Djordjevic while you were in the hospital?" The witness, Mr. Trajkovic, answered: "I learned later that Mr. Simovic -- when Mr. Djordjevic was informed about this incident, he agreed with Mr. Simovic that this unit be introduced, and we would see later on expecting that they would stay in Podujevo for several days, that we would see later on how to provide transportation for these people. And he went with his driver to Prolom Banja, which is very close to Podujevo, and escorted these men to Podujevo." That's the end of the passage. Now, my question to you,

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Before this unfortunate incident in Podujevo happened, had you been in contact or discussed with General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing true about this is that I went to Prolom Banja to fetch them, and nothing else. On the 27th, Mr. Trajkovic came to OUP Podujevo, and he said that the staff had given its approval for me to go fetch them, and then he left for Belgrade. Mr. Trajkovic was not hopitalised. He was not lying in the hospital as an in-patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 27th of March, did you talk to Mr. Djordjevic before this happened on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to Mr. Djordjevic on the 28th when I informed the MUP staff that I had made my decision and returned the reserve unit and notified Mr. Djordjevic because I couldn't get Trajkovic on the line. I notified them because measures needed to be taken to admit these people or readmit these men on the territory of Serbia and that I wanted to get feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Although you partly anticipated my next question, I would like us to look at page 9093, lines 6 and 7, lines 8 through 11, 12 through 14, and 15 through 18. The Prosecutor asked: "While you were in the hospital, did you receive any information about what happened with these men on the 28th of March, 1999, at Podujevo?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TRAJKOVIC ANSWERED
utterances.text: "I think we are talking about the 27th of March because they were introduced just after I was taken to the hospital, unless I'm mistaken, but I think all this took place on the same day, and it was the 27th." The next question: "Very well, but there was just around that time an incident in Podujevo involving these men. Did you learn about the incident while you were in the hospital?" And Mr. Trajkovic answered: "Yes, I learned about it on the next day, on the 28th. I can't remember who the officer was who came to visit me, but he informed me about what had happened just after their arrival, the arrival of this combat group to Podujevo." The next question to you, sir, is: After he was injured, did Mr. Trajkovic spend any time in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I said before in my evidence, Mr. Trajkovic came to OUP Podujevo on the 27th around 5.00 p.m. He talked to me and Mr. Stalevic and then on the same day, he left Kosovo and went to Belgrade to organise the funeral of the late Aleksic. So the best of my knowledge, Trajkovic was never hopitalised. On the 27th, he had just been taken to the hospital in Pristina to have a detailed check-up and then he immediately went on to Belgrade, and I met him in Belgrade at the funeral of the late Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a statement on page 9107, lines 9 to 13. "Djordjevic requested a report because I previously noted that reports about the incident in Podujevo were also written by Mr. Simovic as the commander of the Belgrade SAJ and Mr. Stalevic as the commander of the Pristina SAJ, as they were two directly superior officers who were there at the time when the incident happened." Mr. Simovic, did you write any report about the events in Podujevo of the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The event or incident of the 28th of March, 1999 was not covered in any report written by either me or Mr. Stalevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Simovic, thank you for answering my questions. Your Honours, I have now completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I had imagined that we would not have to proceed with this witness so soon. In any case, I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, just a couple of background questions. You told us earlier that you graduated from a school, and the record indicates a school of defectology. What course did you do, and which school did you graduate from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a course. I completed the secondary school for Internal Affairs, the high school of Internal Affairs, and also the faculty of defectology.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And when was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I completed high school or secondary school in 1979, and I started to work as a rookie police officer. I completed my high school, I think, in 1992, and then I graduated from university for learning disability 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. When the SAJ was re-established -- or I should just ask you this question first. In 1996 the minister Sokolovic made or issued an order, a decision, to re-establish the SAJ, and maybe it could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: D401. Is the system working?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think, Mr. Djurdjic explained that this was, in fact, a re-establishment of the SAJ, but you didn't testify to that. Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. SAJ, S-A-J, was formed in 1992, and it had the same powers and the same units in 1992. There was also a command with three units. By adopting the decision in 1996, the minister of Internal Affairs, Mr. Sokolovic, placed all the other decisions out of effect, so there isn't much difference between 1992 and 1996 in the forces themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in 1996, to whom did Mr. Trajkovic report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: As the commander of the special anti-terrorist unit SAJ was there in 1992 right until the end, Mr. Trajkovic. Since the unit was part of the public security sector, he reported to the chief of the sector, but the order for the unit to go into action can only come from the minister. The minister makes the decision, and the chief of the sector would deal with its actual deployment or actions, if you understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, the minister set the overall policy, framework, and decided that the SAJ could be mobilised, but once they were mobilised by the minister's decision, Mr. Trajkovic would report to the chief of sector, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Like I said, only the minister can order the engagement of the SAJ. The decision is implemented by the chief of the sector. He would convey the minister's decision to the commander, to Trajkovic, and Trajkovic would decide which unit and how many members would be used for any particular task. And I can give you an example, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, so you are saying that the minister decided on the engagement, and the chief of the sector was merely a conduit, a lubricated conduit just to transfer that decision to Mr. Trajkovic. What other role apart from communicating the minister's decision did the chief of the public security department have in respect to the operations of a SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the sector, because he couldn't engage the SAJ units without the permission of the minister and was the immediate superior to the SAJ, would implement all the requests of the SAJ and would assist in all possible assignments that the SAJ had, whether this was training or equipping, upgrading and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. You testified earlier that in respect to the engagement of the Skorpions, that group of reservists -- well, before I go to the question, did you know that they were referred to as the Skorpions, because that's what I will call them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that they were referred to as Skorpions. In a conversation with Mr. Trajkovic when we discussed the reserve forces and when he said that a person by the name of Mrgud was the one that they spoke to about that, that those members who would join the MUP reserve forces would also include those who were in the unit in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem that was called the Skorpions, but I really didn't have any information about that because I met Mr. Medic for the first time when I went to get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to get to that in due course. I just wanted to find out when you became aware of this name. So it seems to me that you are saying that Mr. Trajkovic told you that they were called the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I heard that from my conversation with Trajkovic, even before they had been admitted to the reserve forces, and up until that time, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Well, you said that when these discussions were taking place to engage these Skorpions into the reserve formation of the SAJ, Mr. Trajkovic spoke with Mr. Djordjevic because he couldn't speak directly to the minister. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that Mr. Trajkovic communicated with the chief of the sector. All I said was that he informed the chief of the sector that he should let the minister know and to see if the minister would permit that or not. I never mentioned the word Skorpions in my testimony or in what -- in what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I ask you again having regard to what you just said that Mr. Trajkovic had to speak or inform the chief, as you put it, to whom did the head of the Skorpions -- sorry. To whom did Mr. Trajkovic, your commander, report, who in the MUP did he report to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Outside of the Kosovo and Metohija territory and beyond the combat area in peacetime conditions, his superior in the MUP was the chief of the sector. With the establishment of the staff in Kosovo and Metohija for anti-terrorist fighting, not only Trajkovic, but all the units in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija were under the jurisdiction of the staff because they were sent there by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll ask you again. To whom did your commander, Trajkovic, report? Who in the MUP? Which individual? He must have had, I understand it based on some evidence we've had before, he must have had a superior officer in the MUP. To whom did he report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said. In regular conditions when it was not an extraordinary situation, his superior was the chief of the sector, General Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to their operations in Kosovo during the war in 1999, to whom did he report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Commander Trajkovic was the member of the staff which was formed in 1998. I think it was in July, and he was directly responsible to the head of the staff or the staff for anti-terrorist actions in Kosovo and Metohija. This was not only Trajkovic, but all the senior officers who had been sent to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yet when it came to the engagement of these men that I referred to as the Skorpions, he did not go to the minister through Mr. Lukic, he went to the minister through Mr. Djordjevic. Can you tell us why, having regard to your evidence, that these men were to assist you on operations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the staff was informed with that, and they were in agreement. Then Mr. Trajkovic, through the chief of the sector, got in touch or the chief of the sector conveyed to the minister that he should issue an order or decide that the reserve forces should be activated, because as a special unit, we don't have a reserve force. We cannot have our own reserve force, and that is why in a given situation we need to use the reserve forces of the MUP to be reattached to us. So this would not constitute the reserve force of the SAJ, but the reserve force of the MUP, which would be attached to the SAJ, or assigned to the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know that. But these -- you told us that from the 24th of March your unit was sent to Kosovo and Metohija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 23rd. Thanks. And they along with Mr. Stalevic's unit -- both SAJ units were now engaged in operations in Kosovo for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I said that we arrived in the Kosovo and Metohija territory on the 23rd. What is it with Stalevic now? He is a commander of equal status as I so we can function under the united command of Trajkovic. We cannot act independently of Belgrade or Pristina because we were under the same command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "we cannot act independently of Belgrade or Pristina," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I never said that we were acting independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said -- I'll quote what you said, Mr. Simovic. You said "we cannot act independently of Belgrade or Pristina because we were under the same command." What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood. I said that SAJ Pristina and SAJ Belgrade had a united command, and that is the SAJ command. In other words, Mr. Zivko Trajkovic. I don't understand why you mention Mr. Stalevic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All I was asking you earlier was simply that after the 23rd of March, 1999, both your unit and Mr. Stalevic's unit were operational in Kosovo and Metohija for the duration of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I think there was one break when we gave our men some rest in Belgrade, but I can accept that from the 23rd until the end of the war we were in the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what I want to come back to is why, having regard to the fact that you are now engaged in Kosovo and Metohija, was it necessary for Mr. Trajkovic to get the sanction of the minister through Mr. Djordjevic and not Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The engagement of the special unit outside of the territory of Kosovo was something that only the minister could decide. At the same time in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija from the time the MUP staff was established in 1998, the minister transferred his powers to the MUP staff so that this staff set up by the minister was able to engage SAJ in the territory of Kosovo without informing the minister. And this applied to all units in the territory of Kosovo because the minister set up the staff by his own decision, and this staff had all the powers of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand what you mean. When you say "the staff had all the powers of the minister," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was trying to say that if the minister can engage the SAJ outside the territory of Kosovo, then the MUP staff is equally able to engage the SAJ in Kosovo. This MUP staff had both sectors represented in it, the public security and the state security. Do you understand now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you that. Let me get back to the question I was asking you. The MUP staff, according to you, is responsible for the operations in Kosovo and Metohija during the war. And the MUP staff, Mr. Lukic, was the head of the MUP staff. The question is simply this: Why didn't Trajkovic convey his operational needs for this reserve unit to the minister through Mr. Lukic instead of through Mr. Djordjevic as he did? That's all I want to hear. Why go to Mr. Djordjevic when Mr. Lukic was the person you are saying is responsible in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic was in charge of Kosovo but not in charge of Serbia proper, so that the minister had to make a separate decision to activate reservists. Only the minister could make the decision to activate the reserve force of the ministry. Nobody else but the minister could do that because the administration of the police that is in charge of the whole procedure for admitting reservists, and this administration is in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I think we'll move on and return to this. This person who was killed in the -- killed on the 27th of March when Mr. Trajkovic's vehicle struck a mine, what was his name, can you remind us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: The body-guard and driver of Mr. Zivko Trajkovic was killed. His name was Radovan Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he killed on the spot, if you understand what I mean? Killed at about the time when the mine hit the vehicle, or was he -- or did he die later?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I said he was dead on the spot. And his body was transferred to Pristina to the forensic department of the hospital in Pristina. He was transported from Bradas where he was killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know when his body was taken to Belgrade? What date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date, whether it's the 29th, the 28th, or the 30th, I can't be sure. All I know is that I went to attend the funeral. I spent a couple of days in Belgrade, and after the funeral, I returned to Kosovo. But I cannot tell you the exact date of the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, he was killed on the 27th. Was the funeral the next day, two days after, three, four, five days after? Can you approximate? A week after?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I said that. You just don't understand me. This man, Aleksic, got killed on the 27th. From this spot where he was killed, he was transferred to the forensic department of the Pristina hospital. I left for Belgrade on the 28th, and I don't know whether the funeral was on the 29th or the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you are saying his funeral could have been two or three days after he was killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that a postmortem had to be carried out. The body had to be moved to Belgrade for burial. That's why I can't say with any certainty whether the funeral took place on the 29th or the 30th. If you let me, I'll call his family in Belgrade and find out the exact date, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
