utterances.text: Well, we'll get back to the date, but if you have the opportunity to do so, please, because we are going to get back to the date of that funeral. But you will say, Mr. Simovic, that that funeral was not on the 28th of March, the date of the killings at Podujevo? Is that your evidence, that certainly that was not the date of the funeral?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I mean to say that I can't remember whether the funeral was on the 29th or the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So do you say, therefore, that it could not have been on the 28th, that is, the day of the Podujevo incident?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything. I can only say I don't remember the date of the funeral and that it was on the 29th or the 30th. You keep referring me back to the 28th, I'm telling you 29 or 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get to that. What was your relationship with this driver and body-guard of Mr. Trajkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: We were as close as brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long had you known him for?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: For over ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you tell some investigating magistrate or an investigating magistrate in respect to the Podujevo incident that you had to leave on the day of the incident to attend the funeral?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was not just any funeral. It was the funeral of my associate Mr. Aleksic. It's true that I had to say I'm going and I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about the date. Did you tell any magistrate that you left to go to the funeral, that is, you left Podujevo to go to the funeral in Belgrade on 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said I had to go because I was expecting the mortal remains to be transported --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. The question is whether you told them that you left to go to the funeral on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: You have to understand, according to our customs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, Mr. Simovic --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: -- when somebody is very close, you have to stand by the coffin right up to the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you tell the magistrate that you went to his funeral on the 28th? Yes or no? Did you say that? Can you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I left on the 28th to participate in the wake. I said I was going on the 28th to attend the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you are saying now that -- or may I ask you this: Is it possible that your dear friend, as close as a brother, could have had or there could have been a wake for him the day after he was killed, on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: You just don't understand. We still mourn him to this day. A man who lays down his life cannot be mourned for just one day. You mourn him permanently. The funeral took place on the 29th or the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this regard there are quite some documents that I need to show the accused -- show the witness, sorry. And I probably want to take the break a little early to organise my papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be more practical. We will have the second break five minutes early. We will resume at five minutes to 1.00. We'll now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before the witness is brought back, Your Honours, please accept my apology, I thought we were to return at, sorry, at 1.00 actually, so I thought I was on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think your lateness has been compensated, so we will overlook both omissions. As long as it doesn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At least on those occasions when the Chamber is here on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, did you participate in any way in the investigation of the crime that was committed at Podujevo on the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it correct that if crimes are committed by police officers when they are engaged, that the commanding or the superior officer has a duty to collect all relevant information in respect to those crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: My role as the SAJ commander, when something happens in the territory of an OUP of Podujevo or anything, is to report, and I did report to OUP Podujevo, that killings had occurred in Podujevo. I did not see who had fired, nor did any of my unit members see who had committed these crimes. But the competent organ, the OUP Podujevo, did take the necessary follow-up steps and investigation starting with notification of investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you, on the 28th when you went to the scene, ascertain to your own satisfaction that none of your men had seen who fired?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: If any one of my unit members had seen anyone shooting, that person would have been arrested on the spot. Since none of my unit members saw who had fired, all that was done was to give first aid to the survivors, to save those who could be saved, and I reported to OUP Podujevo so that other measures and investigation could be undertaken, which was later done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not talking about other measures now. I'm going to ask you to focus on my question. We have a lot of material to cover, so just please answer the questions I ask you. Is it that you decided that none of your men had seen who had fired because nobody was arrested, or did you do anything that day to satisfy yourself that none of your men had seen who fired?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the scene, because I hadn't been on the scene when the incident happened, I came when it was all over. My unit members, and that means the active duty personnel of the SAJ who were on the spot, had not seen who had done it. I did what I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: And that was to organise help to inform the OUP Podujevo and then the OUP Podujevo was supposed to take certain steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. I am going to ask one more time, please. What, if anything, did you do that day to ascertain whether any of your men had seen who fired?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the scene I found Dr. Dragan Markovic and some of my unit members giving first aid to those injured, and I organised ambulances to transfer those injured to Pristina, and I asked the unit members present if they had seen anyone shooting. They answered no. If I had known at that moment who was the perpetrator, I would certainly have taken certain steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment I did not know and I couldn't do anything at random.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember which unit members you asked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Dragan Markovic, the platoon commander Spasoje Vulevic and some other men whose name escape me at the moment because it was 12 years ago. At this moment I can only give you the names about which I'm sure. I said the same things in the statement that I gave before the investigating judge and before the court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- did Mr. Vulevic say anything to indicate to you that he knew who had done the shooting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Vulevic told me on the spot that members of the reserve had fired those who had arrived by buses in my escort, but he hadn't seen who exactly had done it. He couldn't point his finger at anyone and say this man fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you question any of the reserves who were present near the scene?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the scene, as I just arrived and talked to my own unit members, they told me they couldn't say who had done it, and when Spasoje Vulevic, the commanding officer, asked the reservists if they had seen who had done it, they didn't answer at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you -- you did not interview any of these reservists that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not. I just gave an order that everyone get on the bus so that I can return them to Prolom Banja so that they should be assembled so that all the appropriate investigative steps could be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you cause any of your staff to interview any of those men that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not ask any of my unit members to do that because we were not specialised for that sort of interview. The OUP Podujevo provided the premises and the presence of an investigating judge, conducted an on-site investigation, and from then on the Prosecutor's Office took over and did their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you there when the investigating judge arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You can answer my questions simply. When from the information you received did the investigating judge arrive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: By that time I was no longer there. I don't know when the investigating judge arrived because by that time I had left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did the Prosecutor arrive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, I was in Belgrade. I had informed the MUP staff about what had happened. I had notified OUP Podujevo to take steps because it was in their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. When you returned or before you returned, just bear with me for a moment, the reservists, this unit of reservists, about how many of them were there on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I fetched them from Prolom Banja, and there were about 100 of them, perhaps more than 100. I can't give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What time of day did the shooting of these people occur?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I would hate to make a mistake. It could have been 10.00 or 11.00 a.m. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These reservists at the time when you escorted them to Podujevo, they were under your command, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Not yet. I had only taken them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when you say you took them over, can I take it that means that you were responsible for giving them orders?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told them -- very well. You told them to remain in the buses. You told Mr. Boca, Mr. Slobodan Medic to return them to Prolom Banja, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Before he left for Belgrade, Mr. Trajkovic told me that a certain Slobodan Medic was in some way in charge of those reservists, and when I met Slobodan Medic, it was the first time I laid eyes on the man. And when we moved towards Podujevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are going into a history that I'm not really asking. Did you order Mr. Medic to take them back to Prolom Banja after the incident?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I ordered my officers, or rather, the members of my unit who -- that all the reservists should get back on their buses, and then I went to the Podujevo OUP and told Mr. Medic that he should, together with the reservists, get back on the bus and then from there on to Prolom Banja. The unit of the reserve force had still not been attached or resubordinated to the Belgrade SAJ unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But at that time the members of the unit and Mr. Medic were under your supervision and control?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I only brought them there pursuant to an oral order from Commander Trajkovic because he was the one who was supposed to pick them up, so I contacted this person, Medic, Slobodan, because that's what I was told by my commander, that that is the person to contact, and had these not been MUP reservists, had it been anyone else as a colonel of the MUP, I would certainly have taken this opportunity to send these men back and have the investigation properly conducted and these people brought to justice because what had been done in Podujevo was really unacceptable, not only to me as a human being but professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said: "Had these not been MUP reservists, had it been anyone else, as a colonel of the MUP, I would certainly have taken this opportunity to send these men back and have the investigation properly conducted and these people brought to justice." Would you say, Mr. Simovic, that there was no proper investigation of this incident in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that they were reservists of the Serbian MUP at that point in time. They were not SAJ reservists because the SAJ does not have a reserve force, and they had still not been attached to the SAJ, and in the investigative steps that were taken subsequently, I wasn't there to say -- to be able to say whether it was done properly or not, but I assumed that it was because all of those who were involved in this were actually taken to court and in the end they were also indicted for the acts that they had committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about March and April. Do you know -- did you satisfy yourself in March and in early April when you returned, that there had been a proper investigation and the perpetrators were arrested? Let's say April, early April when you returned.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned, I was at the base where my unit was in Kosovo Polje. I was not in Podujevo so I didn't have any contact with anyone regarding this unfortunate incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So you didn't have any contacts. In your experience, Mr. Simovic, as a policeman, had men under your command, well, you said they weren't under your command, so I'll ask you this: In your experience as a policeman, had men whom you had taken over, as you put it, murdered as many as a dozen civilians, a dozen to 19 civilians including women and children? Has that ever happened in your experience, apart from that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the reserve force who committed this act, and I can say that in my experience, in my practice, I've never experienced any incident of that sort, and that is why at that point in time I did -- I tried to do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you did your best? Very well. Did you discover that morning that these men were alleged to have lined up women and children and executed them with the MUP issued weapons, high-powered weapons from point-blank range? Did you discover that that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, I was not present. I only said -- I just said how long I had stayed in Podujevo and how long that stay of mine lasted. So when I came to the site and determined and established what I could, I put them back on the buses, I went to the police department, and returned to make sure that they would head for Belgrade and then I left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Please don't repeat that mantra. I'm asking you, did you you discover that day as you tried your best, as you put it, that these reservists that you had taken over had lined up women and children and shot them at point-blank range? Did you discover that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not get any information from my members that anyone had lined people up and shot them because had any of my men seen that, I would certainly have reacted. So I did and acted pursuant to the information that I was able to obtain from my men who were on site, and as an officer, I informed the OUP so that they would take the necessary steps because it was within their jurisdiction because I did not have the professional staff that would be capable of conducting an on-site investigation. That kind of investigation would have to be conducted by an organ in the territory where the act had been committed. My unit was an anti-terrorist unit, and we did not have in our ranks investigators, special forensic technicians and so on. We didn't have that kind of profile of police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you went on the scene or at any time that day, did you discover approximately how many victims there were? And remember, you said that you were doing your best. Did you discover how many women and children were murdered that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: My men who were on site said that several civilians had been killed. I could not go and count the bodies because in that way I could actually destroy the trace evidence that was there, so I just asked how many victims there were and they said they didn't know, they said there were several. What I did is when I saw that there were survivors, I did everything I could in order to save those civilians. I believe there were four injured persons, and I'm glad to say that they were all saved and they are alive and well to this day, and I'm happy for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where did you first see these survivors?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I'm not sure if I understood you correct. Did you ask me whether I saw them later on afterwards, or whether I saw them there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, you saw survivors there. Where did you first see them? Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was near the courtyard. Dr. Dragan was administering first aid to a civilian, and one of my members was carrying a child towards the ambulance. This was in an area between the road and the courtyard of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are saying that you knew that persons had been murdered in the courtyard and you did not look inside the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you why I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: In order not to trample on the trace evidence. So I was really trying hard, and that's why I went to Podujevo immediately in order to ensure that the site was secured because that's absolutely necessary in order to make sure that when the investigation is conducted, the -- it can be established what had happened. And I am saying again that I did whatever was possible at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. How many people were killed at Podujevo by these reservists that you took over?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know the number at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe about 19 people. I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you discover in the course of doing your best that it was approximately 19 people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I heard of that only later on when an investigation was started or instigated against the perpetrators of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was this that you discovered that the men, these men had killed 19 people? When?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I did not discover it myself. I only learned that later on when the trial was -- actually proceedings were started against Demirovic and Sasa, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know when this was? Can you tell us which year, for example, did you learn that these men that you took over had killed 19 civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I really cannot. Twelve years on and after all the work that I have behind me, I really can't remember the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we, Your Honours, have a look at document with 65 ter number 06118.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could start by looking at the front page. I don't think we have a translation of the front page, of the first page. But does that indicate that this is a record of the trial in the Prokuplje district court against Sasa Cvjetan and Dejan Demirovic on 9th of October, 2002? You can see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It is a note on the main trial, or record of the main trial in Prokuplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You remember you testified at that trial?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like us to move to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the time being we only have a translation of -- we had to do a translation on a priority basis because of certain pressures in the Tribunal with the translators, so we only have a translation of those parts which the Prosecution wanted to show to the Court, but the entire document is in B/C/S and has been disclosed to the Defence, so they have the remainder of it. If we could move to page 2 in the English, which is page 31 in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you were at the staff in Podujevo to make arrangements. And if you could look at the middle of the page in English, I'll just read it: "I don't know exactly how long the meeting lasted. In any case, at some point during the meeting we heard automatic fire. I can't remember now all the weapons that were fired because it is difficult to define precisely as it depends on the conditions, the location, the position, and the distance. In any case, I immediately went to the scene where I found Dragan Markovic helping the wounded civilians." Do you see that part? Do you have that part in front of you, Mr. Simovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can I just see the last sentence so that I can find that area? Could you quote the last sentence -- the sentence before the portion that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm speaking about where you said: "I immediately went to the scene where I found Dr. Dragan Markovic helping the wounded civilians."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I can just find the "immediately", that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance to the witness, that's the fifth line from the top, Mr. Simovic: "I don't know exactly." Now, I don't know which portion Mr. Stamp was referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Stamp's portion begins three or four lines lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, if you look 12 lines down you see where you referred to finding Dr. Markovic helping the wounded civilians.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You went on to say: "He was a physician for our unit, I mean the Belgrade SAJ. He was a doctor of the SAJ unit. I took measures to provide an ambulance and ensure the quickest possible transfer to a medical institution where further treatment was to be provided. The scene was really crowded with members of different units all mixed together. I did not enter the area where the civilians were killed because professional medical care was being provided there." Let's stop there. You told this Court that you did not even go to look because you did not want to displace forensic traces. You told that court then that it was because people were being treated. Which reason is true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You gave to this Court one reason for not even looking to see the bodies in the courtyard. And the reason you gave to this Court was that you did not want to interfere with the evidence, with the crime scene. You told the other court, this court that I'm directing you to, that the reason that you didn't even look in to see who had been killed or how many was because medical care was being provided there. Which reason is true, what you told the Prokuplje court or what you told this Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Both reasons are true. Both of them. That I organised the -- us providing assistance to these people and also to make sure that the trace evidence was not displaced and to secure the crime scene because if you are listening carefully to what I said, everything that I had said earlier is actually repeated here, but of course, I cannot use the same exact words in my statement then and now 12 years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, the record clearly shows that you gave completely different reasons. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I've said here is that I did not go to see the bodies in order to prevent the destruction of trace evidence. And as I said, one of the reasons too was that I tried to save lives, so both these reasons, if you understand what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was providing professional medical care?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Professional medical care was provided by Dr. Dragan Markovic. He was the doctor with the SAJ unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted to know the name. You must just focus on the questions I ask you and answer them, otherwise we'll be here the whole week. Was he alone in that place providing medical care in that courtyard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Professional medical care was provided by him because he was a doctor, Dragan Markovic, but I already mentioned his name earlier, he was the SAJ doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he the only person in the courtyard? That's the question. Was he the only person in the courtyard providing professional medical care?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Dragan was the only professional there, the only doctor there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you about professionals, I wasn't asking you about -- well, I did use the expression professional medical care. So I'll ask you this: Was he the only person in the courtyard giving assistance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I have listened very carefully to your words, and I always try to answer your questions. You asked about professional medical care. Dr. Dragan was the professional, but other SAJ members assisted him in providing medical assistance. They would pass on his bag to him or hold the IV bottle. You are not listening carefully to my words. Dr. Dragan was the only doctor there who was providing medical assistance, and he was being helped by active-duty SAJ members who were there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about in the courtyard where the civilians were killed. This what you said: "I did not enter the area where civilians were killed because professional medical care was being provided there." Is it your evidence that Dr. Markovic was in the courtyard providing medical assistance and was assisted by members of the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Dr. Dragan was providing professional medical assistance. As far as I can recall, it was on the side of the road and not where the bodies were. The wounded had been transferred. They had been taken to a place by the road, but I can't quite recall every detail. It has been 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But this is an important detail. This is where the bodies were of the most extraordinary incident in your career, or one of them. You said, I'll read it again: "I did not enter the area where the civilians were killed because professional medical care was being provided there." Did Dr. Markovic provide professional medical help in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really state that with certainty. I can't say with certainty whether this was happening in the courtyard or on the side of the road. And I don't know how to describe to you what that looked like, where the courtyard was, where the building was, and where the road was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you don't know if Dr. Markovic provided any medical help to anybody in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the doctor provided professional medical assistance and saved four people. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about the courtyard, Witness. Do you know if any medical assistance was provided by the doctor in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, I'm not sure whether this was in the courtyard or outside of it, but professional medical assistance was being given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said further: "This is why I immediately called the commander of the Skorpions Slobodan Medic and ordered him to gather his unit and return to Prolom Banja." You told the Court today more than once to my questions that you did not give Medic or any of these men orders. Your expression was you just took them over. Is it not true, sir, that you were responsible for these men to the extent that you could give them orders, or were you lying when you testified in Prokuplje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I state here with full responsibility that they were not under my command and that they had not been subordinated attached to the SAJ, that is how it was then and I repeat the same now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you order -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation that I received from the record that Mr. Stamp is quoting, I heard that it was said, translated, he did not order Medic to return. And I don't know what you mean by lies because as I read the Serbian version of this record, I don't want to actually interfere, but I think what is put to the witness should be put to them fairly and exactly as recorded in this record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was reading from the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are already six minutes over time, Mr. Stamp. We've been trying to allow you to reach a logical point, but I think it's going too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think tomorrow you should, if you wish, return to this subject, have the witness read the passage in the statement, and then the passage in his evidence, which you say is different, and get his comment. But that can be done tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Could it since it has been shown it to the witness and he said he testified there, could it be received in evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long is this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it's about 35 pages in the original. However, at least in respect to this witness, I don't imagine the Prosecution is interested in more than five pages, but there are other witnesses that it might relate to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At this moment you've only put to the witness something like a quarter of a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will not receive the whole document as a matter of convenience. The transcript will reveal that quarter of a page. If it is that you are going to deal a with a lot more of the document, the position may change.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. We must adjourn, and we continue tomorrow, Mr. Simovic. We resume tomorrow at 2.15. A Court Officer will assist you during the adjournment. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of April 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.52 p.m.
